title: CBRNE III: Biological & Radiological/Nuclear
learningObjectives: Recognize bioterrorism clues and match Category A agents to transmission and PPE.
Separate radiation EXPOSURE from CONTAMINATION and act accordingly.
Apply time–distance–shielding and emergency-worker dose guidance.
Manage dirty-bomb casualties without delaying trauma care.

summary.title: Biological Events Arrive Quietly
summary.content: There's usually no scene — just a surge of sick people at EDs and clinics days later. Clues: clusters of the same severe illness, illness in an unusual place/season/age group, many cases from one event or location, sick or dead animals, a single case of a vanished disease (smallpox = public-health emergency). Overt events (threat letters, sprayers) are the exception. EMS role: protect yourself (PPE), mask the patient (source control), limit crew exposure, notify public health/medical control, clean the vehicle, follow prophylaxis guidance.

summary.title: CDC Category A Agents — EMS Essentials
summary.content: ANTHRAX (inhalational): flu-like → severe respiratory distress, shock, widened mediastinum; NOT person-to-person → standard precautions. PLAGUE (pneumonic): fulminant pneumonia ± hemoptysis; person-to-person by DROPLETS → mask the patient, droplet precautions (many systems use N95). SMALLPOX: high fever then synchronous pustules, densest on face/extremities incl. palms/soles; AIRBORNE + CONTACT → N95/PAPR, gown, gloves, eye protection; vaccinate contacts early. BOTULISM: alert patient with descending symmetric flaccid paralysis (diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia → respiratory failure), no fever; not person-to-person; support ventilation, antitoxin. TULAREMIA: pneumonia/ulceroglandular, not person-to-person. VIRAL HEMORRHAGIC FEVERS (e.g., Ebola): fever, bleeding, shock; CONTACT/droplet with body fluids → full PPE with trained donning/doffing and a spotter.

summary.title: Radiation: Exposure vs Contamination
summary.content: EXPOSED (irradiated): energy passed through the body — like an X-ray. The patient is NOT radioactive and poses NO risk to you. CONTAMINATED: radioactive material is ON (external) or IN (internal: inhaled, ingested, wounds) the body — risk is mainly from spreading particles. Standard PPE (gloves, gown, N95/surgical mask, eye protection) + removing the patient's clothing (removes the large majority of external contamination) + gentle washing handles most of it. Radiation contamination is almost never an immediate threat to the patient's life or yours — treat life threats FIRST.

summary.title: Time, Distance, Shielding
summary.content: Minimize TIME near a source; maximize DISTANCE (inverse-square law: double the distance → ¼ the dose); use SHIELDING (concrete, earth, vehicles, buildings). Wear personal dosimeters and know turn-back values. US EPA emergency-worker guidance: ~5 rem (50 mSv) for general emergency actions, ~10 rem (100 mSv) to protect valuable property, ~25 rem (250 mSv) for lifesaving/protecting large populations — higher only by fully informed volunteers. ALARA: As Low As Reasonably Achievable.

summary.title: Device Types & Field Medicine
summary.content: RDD ('dirty bomb'): conventional explosive + radioactive material — the blast injures; radiation doses are usually low; triage and treat trauma normally, then decon. RED (radiological exposure device): hidden source irradiating passers-by — exposures without contamination, often discovered by clusters of skin burns/ARS. IND (nuclear detonation): blast, thermal, prompt radiation, then fallout — public messaging is 'Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned' (shelter in the center of a sturdy building/basement until advised). Acute radiation syndrome: earlier vomiting = higher dose (roughly: < 1 h → severe dose, > 4 h → likely survivable). Potassium iodide (KI) protects ONLY the thyroid and ONLY against radioactive iodine — not a general 'radiation pill'.

clinicalPearls: An irradiated patient is not radioactive. A contaminated patient is — but clothing off + wash fixes most of it.
Never delay lifesaving trauma care for radiological decontamination.
Mask the coughing patient first — source control beats PPE.
Smallpox, Ebola, and pneumonic plague are the Category A agents that spread person-to-person; anthrax, botulism, tularemia do not.
White-powder letters are usually hoaxes: don't shake/sniff, isolate the area, wash hands with soap and water, call law enforcement/HazMat.
redFlags: Multiple previously healthy adults with severe pneumonia and shock from the same building.
Fever + synchronous pustules on face and palms → smallpox until proven otherwise.
Alert patient with descending paralysis and difficulty swallowing → botulism; prepare for respiratory failure.
Unexplained radiation-like skin burns in several people → hidden source (RED).
commonMistakes: Refusing to touch an irradiated (exposed-only) patient.
Giving KI after a dirty bomb without radioiodine involvement.
Using only standard precautions for smallpox or VHF.
Over-decontaminating stable patients while critical trauma waits.
memoryAids: Category A: 'A-B-P-S-T-V' — Anthrax, Botulism, Plague, Smallpox, Tularemia, VHF.
Exposed = X-ray (safe). Contaminated = mud (wash it off).

decisionTrees.title: Radiological Casualty
decisionTrees.content:
Radiological incident suspected
  → Life threats? YES → treat now (standard PPE), decon after/with care
  → Contaminated?
       Unknown/likely → survey if meter available; remove clothing; gentle wash; cover wounds
       Exposed only → no decon needed; patient is NOT radioactive
  → Early vomiting? (< ~1 h) → high dose → priority for hospital ARS care
  → Track your dose: time, distance, shielding; dosimeter turn-back values
